experiments.title: Who gets the drink?
experiments.hook: Swap one name and find the few parts of the model that track who's who.
experiments.why: It's one of the few behaviors researchers have traced almost head by head: about two dozen attention heads in GPT-2 small.
experiments.prompt: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to

patching.clean: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to
patching.corrupted: When Mary and John went to the store, Mary gave a drink to

lookFor: Check Predictions first. GPT-2 small should favor ·Mary (the dot means the word starts with a space), the person who didn't do the giving.

In Swap test, press Run swap test. Pry copies one attention head at a time from the original sentence into the changed one, and measures how much each swap raises the score for ·Mary. A bigger blue number means more of the answer came back.

Each square's one head: rows are layers 0 to 11, columns are heads 0 to 11. Blue squares bring ·Mary back, orange ones push it further away, and pale ones don't do much. Click a square to see its numbers.
Expect most squares to stay pale. A small number of heads, mostly in the later layers, carry most of the effect.

found.summary: Wang et al. traced this exact kind of sentence in GPT-2 small and described a circuit of about two dozen attention heads. Some find the repeated name, some suppress it, and a group they called "name mover" heads (in layers 9 and 10) copy the other name to the output. They also say it isn't the whole story of how the model does it.

citations.label: Wang et al. 2022, Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small

next.reset: Press Back to normal to clear the swap pair and close this guide. It won't touch your prompt.
next.try: Next, try Knock out the name movers to switch those heads off and see if the answer survives.

experiments.title: Knock out the name movers
experiments.hook: Knock out (switch off) three heads from the paper and see if the model notices.
experiments.why: The paper found these three heads do most of the name moving, and that when they're knocked out, other "backup" heads partly take over.
experiments.prompt: When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to
lookFor: Pry's already knocked out three heads in the Attention tab: layer 9, head 9; layer 9, head 6; and layer 10, head 0. They show as red squares with an x in Expert view (the grid).
Press Run Ablated (3) above the grid, then compare Original top-5 with Ablated top-5. Does ·Mary (the dot means the word starts with a space) lose ground, and by how much?
Don't be surprised if the answer survives. Big networks often have spare parts.

found.summary: In the same study, Wang et al. identified these three (layer 9, head 9; layer 9, head 6; layer 10, head 0) as the main name mover heads. When they knocked them out, other heads they called "backup name movers" partly took over, so the drop was smaller than you might expect. Pry switches heads off by setting their output to zero, while Wang et al. mostly replaced it with an average, so treat your numbers as a rough echo, not a replication.

citations.label: Wang et al. 2022, Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small

next.reset: Press Back to normal, or press Ablation ON to turn the knockout off. Either way, you'll get the Lines view back.
next.try: Next, try Who gets the drink? to find the same heads by swapping names.

experiments.title: Spot the copycat heads
experiments.hook: Repeat a made-up phrase and watch the model look back to copy what came next.
experiments.why: These copying heads turn up in many models, and the researchers argue they're an important part of how a model learns from the text in front of it.
experiments.prompt: Pip ordered zebra lamps from Quorn. Pip ordered zebra lamps from
lookFor: The model's never seen this phrase, so the only way to guess the last word is to look back at the first copy. Check Predictions for ·Qu, the start of Quorn (the dot means the word starts with a space).
Press Find copying heads at the top of the Attention panel. Pry tests every head on a repeated random sequence and rings the ones that copy, such as layer 5, head 1 and layer 5, head 5.

Press Back to your prompt. Then pick layer 5, head 1 (or head 5) with the Layer and Head menus above the lines, or click that square in Expert view to see its whole pattern. On the second copy, the last word looks back at ·Qu, the word that came after ·from the first time.

found.summary: Olsson et al. named these "induction heads": heads that find an earlier copy of the current word and attend to the word that came after it, so it can be copied forward. They found them in many models, and argue (with strongest evidence in small models) that they're an important part of how models learn from their context.

citations.label: Olsson et al. 2022, In-context Learning and Induction Heads

next.reset: Press Back to your prompt to leave the copying-heads view, or Back to normal to close this guide too.
next.try: Next, type any sentence twice in a row, press Run, and see if it's the same heads that light up.

experiments.title: Watch it make up its mind
experiments.hook: Peek at the model's best guess after every layer, not just the last one.
experiments.why: On GPT-2 the guesses often sharpen bit by bit toward the final answer, but the early layers can be misleading, so read them as a rough hint.
experiments.prompt: Michael Jordan played the sport of
lookFor: Each row's a layer (layer 0 at the bottom) and each column is a word. Read the last column, under ·of (the dot means the word starts with a space). That's what the model would guess next if it had to stop at that layer.
Indigo cells already match the final answer, and brighter means more sure. Gray cells guess something else.
The early rows guess filler words like ·the. Around layer 7 a sport shows up, but it's ·baseball. From layer 8 on, ·basketball takes the top spot.
The model's most sure around layer 9 and a little less sure at the very end. The last layers often soften a confident guess.

found.summary: nostalgebraist introduced this "logit lens" on GPT-2 and found its guesses often sharpen gradually toward the final answer across layers. Later work showed the plain logit lens can be misleading, especially in early layers and other models, and proposed a trained variant (the tuned lens). So read the early rows as a rough hint.

citations.label: nostalgebraist 2020, interpreting GPT: the logit lens
Belrose et al. 2023, Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens

next.reset: There's nothing to undo here. Press Back to normal to close this guide.
next.try: Next, type your own fact in the Prompt box, like "The Eiffel Tower is in the city of", press Run, and find the layer where the answer shows up.

experiments.title: Where does it keep facts?
experiments.hook: Swap Michael Jordan for Tom Brady and see which layers carry the sport.
experiments.why: In larger GPT models, researchers found that MLP layers in the middle of the network mattered most for recalling facts.
experiments.prompt: Michael Jordan played the sport of

patching.clean: Michael Jordan played the sport of
patching.corrupted: Tom Brady played the sport of

lookFor: This one swaps MLP layers instead of attention heads. An MLP is the part of each layer that works on each word by itself, where many facts seem to be stored. Press Run swap test in Swap test.

The original sentence makes the model say ·basketball (the dot means the word starts with a space), and the changed one says ·football. Each bar copies one layer's MLP from the Michael Jordan sentence and shows how much that raises the score for ·basketball. Blue bars help, orange bars push the other way.
Expect the layer 0 bar to win by a mile. Layer 2 also brings back a good chunk, and the last layer pushes the other way.

That big layer 0 bar is expected. Pry copies a layer at every word at once, and layer 0's MLP acts a lot like part of the word lookup, so copying it basically puts Michael Jordan back into the sentence. It doesn't mean the fact lives there. The researchers below restored one spot at a time, at the last word of the name, in bigger models, and that's how they found the middle layers.

found.summary: Meng et al. used a similar "restore one piece" trick (they called it causal tracing) on larger GPT models and found that MLP layers in the middle of the network, at the last word of the subject, mattered most for recalling facts. Pry patches each layer at every position at once and uses a much smaller model, so expect a blurrier picture than theirs.

citations.label: Meng et al. 2022, Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT (ROME)

next.reset: Press Back to normal to clear the swap pair and close this guide. It won't touch your prompt.
next.try: Next, switch Patch type to Residual and press Run swap test again to see which word's carrying the fact.

experiments.title: Can it count years?
experiments.hook: "From 1732 to 17..": find the layers that know the end year must be bigger.
experiments.why: Researchers found that in GPT-2 small, MLP layers near the end of the network (roughly layers 8 to 11) push up the years bigger than the start year.
experiments.prompt: The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17

patching.clean: The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17
patching.corrupted: The war lasted from the year 1701 to the year 17

lookFor: Check Predictions first. The model should lean toward two-digit endings bigger than 32. It won't be perfect.
The changed sentence starts in 1701, which tells the model almost nothing, because nearly any later year fits. Press Run swap test in Swap test.
The bar at the top says what each sentence predicts. Each bar below copies one layer's MLP from the 1732 sentence and shows how much that raises the score for the original answer.
What to expect: the biggest blue bars should sit in the last few layers (8 to 11), the layers the researchers found push up years bigger than the start. Earlier layers shouldn't do much.

found.summary: Hanna et al. studied this exact setup in GPT-2 small. They found a few attention heads that move the start year to the end of the sentence, and MLP layers near the end of the network (roughly layers 8 to 11) that push up the years bigger than the start. They used the same model but a more targeted kind of patching than Pry's, so your picture may be blurrier. Pry tracks only the single year the model picked, while Hanna et al. added up the chance of every bigger year, so expect a rougher picture.

citations.label: Hanna et al. 2023, How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?

next.reset: Press Back to normal to clear the swap pair and close this guide. It won't touch your prompt.
next.try: Next, change 1732 to 1785 in the Original prompt box, press Run swap test, and see if it's the same layers that light up.

experiments.title: He or she?
experiments.hook: See which parts of the model push a pronoun one way or the other.
experiments.why: Researchers studying gender bias in GPT-2 found the effect was concentrated in a small part of the network, such as a handful of attention heads.
lookFor: In Predictions, see how likely ·she and ·he are (the dot means the word starts with a space).
Why (DLA) only explains the top guess, so it can't compare two words. Blue bars pushed toward it and orange bars pushed against it. The biggest bars pushed hardest.
DLA only counts direct pushes on the answer. A part that helps by setting up later parts won't show up here.
To compare with doctor, press Compare at the top, put "The doctor said that" next to "The nurse said that", and press Run both. Then check how ·she and ·he moved.

found.summary: Vig et al. studied gender bias in GPT-2 with prompts like this one, using causal methods. They found the effect was concentrated in a small part of the network, such as a handful of attention heads. The trick behind the Why tab, splitting the answer into each part's direct contribution, comes from Elhage et al.'s 2021 paper on reading transformers.

citations.label: Vig et al. 2020, Causal Mediation Analysis for Interpreting Neural NLP: The Case of Gender Bias
Elhage et al. 2021, A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits

next.reset: There's nothing to undo here. Press Back to normal to close this guide, and press Compare again to leave Compare mode.
next.try: Next, stay in Compare and try other jobs, like "The engineer said that".

experiments.title: Turn up a concept
experiments.hook: Find a learned concept inside the model, then dial it up and see what it writes.
experiments.why: Many features match a single human-readable idea, and researchers showed that turning one up can steer what a model says.
experiments.prompt: On our trip we walked along the beach and watched the ocean
lookFor: The Features tab lists the concepts the feature dictionary (SAE) found on each word. Click ·ocean or ·beach in the word chips (the dot means the word starts with a space) and read the labels.
Another AI wrote the labels by reading examples, and labels written by an AI can be wrong. Some fit nicely and some don't make much sense.
Note the # number of a feature you liked. Open Steering, pick that # in the Feature menu, drag Steering strength to about 10 to 15, and press Run Steered.
Pry highlights the words that changed. Does the text drift toward that concept? If nothing moves, try a bit more strength or a different feature.

found.summary: Bricken et al. showed that a sparse autoencoder can split a model's activity into many "features", many of which match a single human-readable idea. Templeton et al. scaled this up to a production model and showed that turning a feature up can steer what the model says (their "Golden Gate Bridge" demo). The features in Pry come from openly released sparse autoencoders for GPT-2 small, not from those papers.

next.reset: If the text turns to mush, you've turned it up too far, so lower Steering strength. Press Back to normal to close this guide.
next.try: Next, use Find a concept in Steering to look for a concept that isn't in your prompt.
